newsitem.title: BELGIUM: French squabble over Euro has wider implications.
newsitem.headline: French squabble over Euro has wider implications.

text.p: Internal French squabbling over the rival merits of a strong or weak Euro could poison already tense wrangling between France and Germany over how Europe's single currency should be managed.

The heated exchanges between former French President Valery Giscard d'Estaing, who favours a decoupling of the franc from the mark when the exchange rates to the Euro are set, and the government are causing concern in Brussels.

That such a debate should even have surfaced in France has surprised many, in particular diplomats from the "mark zone" countries which have long been converted to the idea of a Euro at least as strong as the mark.

These countries, among them the three Benelux states, have been astonished to hear the former president providing grist for the mill of the right- and left-wing Eurosceptics in a country which Germany feels is essential to the single currency.
But even the most orthodox monetary experts agree that the question is worth asking, even if they don't always like the answers.

"There is confusion between the decision on European parities, which will be taken by those joining the Euro (at the beginning of 1998), and the parity between the Euro and the dollar, which is the real problem and which will be decided by the markets and the exchange rate policy of the European Central Bank," one expert said.
"But the debate is really about German fundamentalism."

Since German unification, the debate has set those who want the franc to track the mark, whatever the cost, because monetary stability pays dividends, against those who believe it is dangerous to follow a Bundesbank obsessed by the fear of a return of inflation in other countries.
Will the European Central Bank (ECB) follow in the footsteps of the Bundesbank whose primary mission to to ensure price stability so that the Euro is strong? For Germany, the answer is clear.
"We want a stable currency; we do not want to slide into a soft currency scenario," German Chancellor Helmut Kohl told a budget debate in the German parliament on Wednesday.
"That is not arrogance, but comes from 50 years of experience in Germany," he said.
For Giscard d'Estaing, the dogmatic insistence on having a strong Euro risks putting a lasting stranglehold on growth in a European Union weakened in relation to the dollar.

While rejecting his arguments for decoupling the franc from the mark, Prime Minister Alain Juppe has nevertheless agreed that some mechanisms of economic and monetary union would need to be clarified with Germany.
"The Euro is firstly a political gamble. It's not a toy for central bank governors," he said in a statement which strayed from the Bonn line that the Euro must in no way be politicised.
The independence of the future central bank may be a sacred cow but France believes that will not give it the sole right to decide the exchange rate policy of the future Euro zone.
"Because stability may be good, but it's not enough," Juppe said on Wednesday, adding that the ECB could not take the place of governments.
"We need stability, growth and employment," he said.
So the 15 EU member states -- their finance ministers and leaders -- will have a role to play in the management of the single currency alongside the ECB to push their growth and employment goals.
This has long been a goal of France. The idea of "economic government" was raised right at the start of the 1990s, only to be shot down by the Germans.

Paris is currently trying to revive the idea, albeit in a revised form, during discussions on the stability pact which Germany wants to make sure participants in the single currency continue to meet the membership criteria.

France may be ready to accept heavy sanctions on countries that allow their deficit to slip, but in return it has demanded the creation of a "stability council" of member states to make "recommendations" on monetary policy.
Germany has not said no, but for Bonn one thing is clear -- the ECB will remain totally and absolutely independent of political pressure.
